easy.prompt: What is the mean of the values 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's the median of an evenly spaced symmetric set, not the mean here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the largest value, not the average.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Off by one from the correct average.

easy.prompt: For the sorted data 2, 5, 7, 9, 11, what is the median?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: With five ordered values, the median is the middle observation: 7.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's the mean (34/5), not the median.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's the second value (Q1 region), not the middle.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's the fourth value, not the median.

easy.prompt: Which measure of center is most appropriate for heavily right-skewed income data?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: The mean is pulled toward extreme high earners; the median reflects a typical household better.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Range measures spread, not center.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Extreme high values inflate the mean for skewed income.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Mode alone ignores most of the distribution.

easy.prompt: The interquartile range (IQR) equals…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: IQR is the spread of the middle 50%: third quartile minus first quartile.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: SD uses all deviations from the mean, not quartiles.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Adding quartiles is not a spread measure.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's the full range, not the middle half.

easy.prompt: A histogram displays…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The theoretical PDF of a fitted model without data.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Counts or proportions of observations in contiguous bins along a numeric axis.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Exact pairwise correlations between every variable.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Only categorical bar heights with gaps between unrelated bars.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Histograms group numeric data into bins; bar area/height shows frequency in each bin.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: A histogram summarizes observed data, not a formula alone.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Correlations need scatterplots or matrices, not a single-variable histogram.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Bar charts for categories differ; histogram bins are contiguous on a scale.

easy.prompt: If P(A) = 0.35, what is P(not A) for a simple event A?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Complement rule: P(A^c) = 1 − P(A) = 0.65.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Probabilities cannot exceed 1.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Not derived from the complement rule.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's P(A), not the complement.

easy.prompt: Events A and B are independent. Which identity holds?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Independence means the joint factorizes into marginals.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That omits the overlap term unless events are mutually exclusive.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Equal probabilities are not required for independence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Zero conditional probability means incompatibility, not independence.

easy.prompt: A standard deck has 52 cards. What is P(drawing a heart on one random draw)?
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: There are 13 hearts out of 52 equally likely cards.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Half the deck is not hearts.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 26 is not the deck size.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's one specific rank (e.g., ace), not a suit.

easy.prompt: The law of large numbers says that as sample size increases, the sample mean…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Must exactly equal the population mean after 30 observations.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Tends to get closer to the population mean (under regular conditions).

choices.label: D
choices.body: Is always equal to the sample median.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Averaging stabilizes around the true mean for independent, identically distributed data.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Convergence is probabilistic, not a fixed n=30 identity.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Variability of the mean typically decreases with n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Mean and median need not match, especially when skewed.

easy.prompt: The standard normal distribution has mean 0 and standard deviation…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Z-scores standardize to μ=0, σ=1.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Not the standard normal scale.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Zero standard deviation would be a constant, not a normal curve.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: π is not the standard deviation of Z.

easy.prompt: For a Binomial(n, p) model, which assumption is essential?

choices.label: B
choices.body: The number of trials changes after each success.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Outcomes are continuous and unbounded above.

choices.label: D
choices.body: n independent trials with fixed success probability p and binary outcomes.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Binomial counts successes in n fixed, independent Bernoulli trials.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: p can be any value in [0,1].
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: n is fixed in the standard Binomial.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Binomial outcomes are counts of successes, built from 0/1 trials.

easy.prompt: The empirical rule for an approximately normal distribution states that about 95% of data lie within…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: 68–95–99.7: roughly 95% within two SDs.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: About 68% lie within one SD.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The empirical rule is SD-based, not quartile-based.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: About 99.7% lie within three SDs.

easy.prompt: A right-skewed distribution has a longer tail toward…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Right skew: mean typically exceeds median; extreme high values pull the tail right.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Symmetric distributions have balanced tails.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Skew describes tail shape, not a single point.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That describes left skew.

easy.prompt: A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is interpreted as: if we repeated sampling many times and built intervals the same way, about 95% of those intervals would…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Guarantee the next sample mean is correct.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Prove the null hypothesis is false.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Contain 95% of all future individual observations.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: CI coverage is a long-run property of the procedure, not a 95% chance for one fixed interval after data are seen.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Intervals estimate μ, not a deterministic guarantee for one draw.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Estimation intervals are separate from hypothesis tests.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: A CI targets a parameter (mean), not the middle 95% of individuals.

easy.prompt: All else equal, increasing sample size n makes a confidence interval for μ…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Standard error σ/√n shrinks as n grows, reducing margin of error.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Larger n adds information and typically tightens the interval.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Margin of error depends on n through the standard error.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Larger samples are preferred for precision.

easy.prompt: In a significance test, the null hypothesis H₀ is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The probability that the alternative is true.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The default claim tested for possible rejection using sample evidence.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: We assume H₀ unless data provide strong enough evidence against it.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Hypotheses are statements, not probabilities.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: H₀ is often a status-quo or no-effect statement.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The p-value measures evidence against H₀, it is not H₀.

easy.prompt: A p-value is…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The probability that Hₐ is false.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The probability that H₀ is true after seeing the data.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The probability, assuming H₀ is true, of observing data at least as extreme as what was observed.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The same as the significance level α always.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: p-values are computed under the null; they are not posterior probabilities of H₀.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: p-values do not directly give P(Hₐ false).
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That would be a Bayesian posterior, not a frequentist p-value.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: α is a chosen threshold; p is computed from data.

easy.prompt: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is called…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Type I = false positive (reject true H₀); controlled by α.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Type II is failing to reject a false H₀.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Confidence applies to intervals, not this error label.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Power is 1 − P(Type II), not Type I.

easy.prompt: The correlation coefficient r always lies between…
easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: r measures linear association strength and direction on a bounded scale.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Percent scales are not used for r.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Negative associations produce negative r.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: r is standardized and bounded.

easy.prompt: In a scatterplot of study hours (x) and exam score (y), a positive correlation means…

choices.label: C
choices.body: Higher x tends to occur with lower y.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Higher x tends to occur with higher y.

easy.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
easy.explanation: Positive r: upward trend; causation requires further design, not correlation alone.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Correlation does not establish causation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Positive correlation implies an upward association.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That describes negative correlation.

medium.prompt: A sample has x̄ = 50 and s = 10 with n = 25. What is the standard error of the mean?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's √n, not the SE.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's s, not the SE.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's s/n, not s/√n.

medium.prompt: Data: 3, 3, 5, 7, 7, 7, 9. What are the first quartile Q1 and third quartile Q3 (using the usual inclusive median method)?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Lower half {3,3,5} has median 3; upper half {7,7,7,9} has median 7.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Averaging across halves is not the standard quartile rule here.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Q3 is 7, not 9 (the maximum).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Those are not the medians of the lower/upper halves for this dataset.

medium.prompt: Which statement about variance and standard deviation is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Standard deviation is always larger than the range.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Variance is in squared units; standard deviation restores the original units.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Standard deviation equals mean deviation in every distribution.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Variance can be negative for skewed data.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: s² averages squared deviations; s = √s² returns to the data scale.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: SD can be much smaller than the range.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SD uses squared deviations; mean absolute deviation differs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Variance is a sum of squares; it is nonnegative.

medium.prompt: A z-score of −1.5 for an observation means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The value is 1.5 standard deviations below the mean.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The value is 1.5 units below zero.

choices.label: C
choices.body: The value is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The probability of the value is 0.15.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: z = (x − μ)/σ; negative z is below the mean.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: z is relative to the mean in SD units, not zero on the raw scale.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Positive z would be above the mean.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: z is a standardized position, not a probability.

medium.prompt: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, and A, B are independent. What is P(A ∪ B)?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Not from the inclusion-exclusion formula.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's P(A)+P(B) without subtracting overlap.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's P(A∩B), not the union.

medium.prompt: In a class, 60% are undergraduates and 40% of all students are undergraduates who commute. What is P(commute | undergraduate)?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's P(C∩U), not the conditional.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's P(U), not P(C|U).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the joint proportion of all students, not conditional on U.

medium.prompt: A fair coin is flipped 4 times. What is P(exactly 2 heads)?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's exactly one head (4 ways).
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's an even number of heads, not exactly two.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Too few favorable sequences.

medium.prompt: If X ~ Binomial(10, 0.3), what is E[X]?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's n, not the mean.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's Var(X) = np(1−p), not the mean.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's p, not the expected count.

medium.prompt: Heights in a population are Normal(μ=170 cm, σ=6 cm). Approximately what fraction is between 164 and 176 cm?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: 164 to 176 is μ±σ, so about 68% by the empirical rule.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That needs about μ±3σ.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: μ±σ captures much more than half under a bell curve.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 95% corresponds to about μ±2σ (158–182 here).

medium.prompt: Which change increases the spread of a Binomial(n, p) distribution (holding n fixed)?

choices.label: A
choices.body: Setting p exactly to 0.5 when n > 1.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Replacing binary outcomes with a constant outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Moving p away from 0.5 toward 0 or 1 (while staying between them).

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Variance np(1−p) is maximized at p=0.5; extreme p yields lower variance but more concentration at ends.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: p=0.5 maximizes variance for fixed n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Constants have zero variance.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That changes n, not p alone as asked.

medium.prompt: Sample means from n=100 independent observations with finite variance are approximately normal because of…

choices.label: C
choices.body: The Law of Large Numbers alone

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: CLT: distribution of x̄ approaches Normal as n grows, regardless of population shape (mild conditions).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: CLT statement is about the mean (or sums), not the median.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Skew can persist in small samples; CLT helps means when n is large.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: LLN concerns convergence of x̄ to μ, not the shape of x̄'s sampling distribution.

medium.prompt: A Poisson model with rate λ = 4 per hour is appropriate when…

choices.label: B
choices.body: There are exactly two outcomes per trial with fixed n.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Events occur independently at a constant average rate over time with rare multiplicities in tiny intervals.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The sample size n is at most 30.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Poisson counts rare events in fixed intervals; mean equals variance λ.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Poisson variance is λ.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That describes Binomial, not Poisson.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: n=30 is a rule of thumb for t, not Poisson modeling.

medium.prompt: You have x̄=120, s=15, n=36. A 95% t-interval for μ uses margin of error t*·(s/√n). What is s/√n?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Standard error = 15/√36 = 15/6 = 2.5.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's s, not SE.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's s/n, not s/√n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's √n, not SE.

medium.prompt: Holding data fixed, widening a CI from 90% to 99% confidence will…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Increase the critical multiplier and make the interval wider.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Leave the interval unchanged if n is large.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Remove the need for a standard error.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Always narrow the interval because we are more confident.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Higher confidence demands a larger z or t* and a wider interval.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The critical value still changes with confidence level.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: SE is still required to build the interval.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: More confidence requires a wider interval, not narrower.

medium.prompt: A 95% CI for a proportion based on x=40 successes in n=200 uses a normal approximation. What is p̂?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's x/100, not x/n.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's the standard error √(0.2·0.8/200), not p̂.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's 1/n, not the sample proportion.

medium.prompt: A two-sided z-test of H₀: μ=100 versus Hₐ: μ≠100 at α=0.05 rejects when |z| exceeds…
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Two-sided 95% critical values for z are ±1.96.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's closer to 99% two-sided.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's α, not a critical z value.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the one-sided 5% cutoff.

medium.prompt: A test has power 0.80 against a specific alternative. If H₀ is false in that way, the probability we correctly reject H₀ is…
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: Power = 1 − β = P(reject H₀ | Hₐ true in the stated way).

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's β (Type II error rate) if power is 0.80.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's a common α, not power.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Power below 1 means some chance of missing the effect.

medium.prompt: A p-value of 0.03 at α=0.05 means…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Reject H₀ at the 5% level (assuming a two-sided test setup matches the p-value).

choices.label: C
choices.body: Fail to reject H₀ at the 5% level.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: p < α ⇒ reject H₀ in the standard fixed-α framework.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: p is not P(H₀ true).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 0.03 < 0.05 leads to rejection.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: We do not accept H₀; we fail to reject or reject based on α.

medium.prompt: For least-squares simple regression, the slope b₁ equals r·(s_y/s_x). If r=0.8, s_x=5, s_y=10, what is b₁?
medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Used r·(s_x/s_y) or doubled incorrectly.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's r·s_y, not the slope formula.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Inverted the ratio s_y/s_x.

medium.prompt: R² = 0.64 in a simple linear regression means…

choices.label: A
choices.body: 64% of the variation in y is explained by the linear model in the sample.

medium.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
medium.explanation: R² is the squared correlation in simple regression: fraction of variance explained.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: r could be +0.8 or −0.8 since r²=0.64.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Residuals are not mostly zero; R² measures explained variation.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: R² is not the slope.

hard.prompt: A dataset has mean 100 and median 80. Which statement is most plausible?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The distribution is right-skewed with a few large outliers pulling the mean up.

choices.label: B
choices.body: The distribution is left-skewed with outliers on the low side.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Mean and median must be equal for any numeric data.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Mean > median is typical when a right tail contains extreme high values.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Left skew usually gives mean < median.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Symmetric data would have mean ≈ median.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Skew breaks equality between mean and median.

hard.prompt: Using the 1.5×IQR outlier rule on Q1=20, Q3=40 (IQR=20), values above what threshold are flagged as high outliers?
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Upper fence = Q3 + 1.5·IQR = 40 + 30 = 70.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's Q3 + 0.5·IQR, not 1.5·IQR.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's Q3 + 2·IQR.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's Q3 + IQR, not 1.5·IQR.

hard.prompt: A teacher standardizes two exams: Exam A scores have x̄=70, s=5; Exam B have x̄=80, s=10. A student scored 75 on A and 85 on B. Which z-score is higher?

choices.label: A
choices.body: They are equal because both are 5 points above their means.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Exam B because the raw score is higher.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Exam B because its standard deviation is larger.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Exam A (z=1.0) is higher than Exam B (z=0.5).

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Equal raw gaps do not imply equal z when SDs differ.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Standardization compares relative standing, not raw points alone.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Larger SD shrinks z for the same raw gap above the mean.

hard.prompt: Disease prevalence 1%. Test sensitivity 99%, specificity 95%. For a randomly selected person who tests positive, P(disease | +) is closest to…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's specificity among healthy people, not P(disease|+).
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the prior before the test.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's sensitivity P(+|disease), not the posterior.

hard.prompt: Cards are drawn without replacement from a deck. P(two aces in two draws) equals…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: First ace 4/52; second ace 3/51 given one ace removed.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Independence assumption is wrong without replacement.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That treats draws as independent with replacement.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's only the first draw succeeding.

hard.prompt: Suppose P(A)=0.6, P(B)=0.5, and P(A∩B)=0.4. Are A and B independent?
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Independence requires the joint to factorize; here 0.4 ≠ 0.3.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Sum exceeding 1 shows overlap, not independence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Marginals alone do not prove independence.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: The joint is enough to check the product rule.

hard.prompt: If X ~ Normal(μ=50, σ=10), what is P(X > 60) approximately?
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: 60 is one SD above mean; upper tail above z=1 is about 16%.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's about one SD below to the mean region.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the area below z=1, not above.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's P(X>μ), not P(X>μ+σ).

hard.prompt: For X ~ Binomial(400, 0.5), a normal approximation to P(X ≤ 210) should use a continuity correction of…

choices.label: D
choices.body: Exact binomial cannot be approximated for n=400

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: When approximating P(X≤k), use k+0.5 in the z numerator for the upper-inclusive count.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Skipping +0.5 mis-handles the discrete-to-continuous bridge.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: 209.5 corresponds to P(X≤209), not P(X≤210).
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: n=400 is large enough for a normal approximation.

hard.prompt: Waiting times T ~ Exponential(λ=0.2 per minute) have E[T] and SD[T] equal to…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Exponential mean and SD are both 1/λ = 5 when λ=0.2.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Half of 1/λ is not the Exponential SD.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's 1/λ² related scale, not the mean.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: 0.2 is λ, not the mean.

hard.prompt: A sampling distribution of x̄ has SD 2 when n=16 from a population with σ=8. If n increases to 64 (same population), the new SD of x̄ is…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: That's the old SE; larger n shrinks it.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Would need n=256 with σ=8.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Doubling SD would require smaller n, not larger.

hard.prompt: A 99% CI for μ is (48, 52) using a normal critical value. If everything else stays fixed except confidence drops to 95%, the new interval will be…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Lower confidence uses a smaller z* (about 1.96 vs 2.58), shrinking margin of error.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: You can recompute the interval from the same x̄ and SE.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: 99% is wider than 95% for the same data and method.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Changing confidence changes the critical multiplier.

hard.prompt: Bootstrap percentile intervals for the median are preferred over a naive x̄±z·s/√n interval when…

choices.label: A
choices.body: The data are strongly skewed with small n and the parameter of interest is the median.

choices.label: B
choices.body: You need a CI for the population mean with known σ.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Every dataset has zero skew by definition.

choices.label: D
choices.body: The sample is huge and perfectly normal.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Bootstrap resamples the data to approximate the sampling distribution without normality for the median.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Known-σ z intervals are a different scenario.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Real data are often skewed.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Classic t intervals often suffice for means with large normal samples.

hard.prompt: A two-sample t-interval for μ₁−μ₂ assumes (for the standard pooled-variance version taught early) that…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Both groups are independent random samples with approximately normal populations and equal unknown variances.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Paired measurements within subjects are required.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Sample sizes must be exactly 30 each.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Pooled two-sample t uses sp² combining groups under equal-variance assumption.

wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's a z scenario, not the usual pooled t.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Paired designs use differences and a one-sample t on pairs.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: n=30 is a guideline, not a strict requirement.

hard.prompt: You perform 20 independent tests at α=0.05 with all nulls true. The expected number of false rejections is…
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Expected Type I errors ≈ m·α = 20·0.05 = 1.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Not m·α for m=20.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: That's α per test, not the total expected count.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Would mean every test rejects, not the expectation under true nulls.

hard.prompt: A one-sample t-test for μ with n=15, s=12, x̄=118, H₀: μ=100, two-sided, gives t = (118−100)/(12/√15). What is |t|?
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Uses s instead of SE in the denominator.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: That's the numerator only, not divided by SE.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: That's the raw difference 18 divided by s incorrectly.

hard.prompt: Switching from a two-sided to a one-sided test (same data, same α) will…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Make Type I error exceed α automatically.

choices.label: B
choices.body: Always increase the p-value because less area is tested.

choices.label: C
choices.body: Change only the sample size n.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Decrease the reported p-value (for a directionally consistent effect) and can increase power.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: One-sided puts all α in one tail when the effect direction matches Hₐ.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: α is still controlled at the chosen level.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Halving tails can halve the p-value for the same z in the correct direction.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: The data and n are unchanged; only the alternative tail changes.

hard.prompt: A 95% CI for μ is entirely above 0. For a two-sided test of H₀: μ=0 versus Hₐ: μ≠0 at α=0.05, you should…

choices.label: B
choices.body: Conclude μ equals the upper endpoint exactly

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Equivalence: interval excludes 0 ⇔ two-sided test rejects μ=0 at matching 95% level (normal/t setup).

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: 0 is not inside the CI, so H₀: μ=0 is inconsistent.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: The CI bounds an range, not a point estimate only.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Tests do not yield P(H₀ true).

hard.prompt: A residual plot shows a clear curved pattern (smile shape) while r=0.9. What is the best conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.body: The linear model is perfect because r is large.

choices.label: B
choices.body: A linear model is inadequate despite high r; consider transformation or nonlinear terms.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Correlation proves the relationship is linear.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: r measures linear association; systematic curvature in residuals violates linearity assumptions.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: High r can still miss systematic curvature.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Outliers and curvature can coexist.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: r can be high for monotone nonlinear patterns too.

hard.prompt: In regression, the least-squares line always passes through which point?
hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: The fitted line satisfies ȳ = b₀ + b₁x̄, so it goes through the sample means.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: The line need not touch corner points of the data cloud.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: Extreme points need not lie on the LS line.
wrongAnswerExplanations.d: Only if the means are zero.

hard.prompt: Adding a spurious variable that is pure random noise to a multiple regression will, on average across many samples, tend to…

choices.label: A
choices.body: Make residuals exactly zero for all rows.

choices.label: D
choices.body: Not improve true out-of-sample prediction and can inflate R² in-sample.

hard.hint: Think about the precise definition before picking.
hard.explanation: Extra noise predictors may fit sample idiosyncrasies (higher R²) without real predictive gain.

wrongAnswerExplanations.a: Perfect fit needs as many orthogonal predictors as points, not random noise alone.
wrongAnswerExplanations.b: In-sample R² never decreases when adding predictors.
wrongAnswerExplanations.c: Noise variables are usually insignificant.
